prompt:
Write an essay of about 800 words on the subject below.

Write it the way an excellent, idiosyncratic human essayist would: someone with real expertise and strong opinions, writing in the first person for their own blog. Commit to a specific thesis that a thoughtful reader might disagree with. Use concrete particulars (names, numbers, incidents, things only someone who had done the work would know) in place of general statements. Vary sentence length. No headings, no bullet points, no summary paragraph at the end, and none of the stock phrases of AI writing.

Output only the essay, with no title.

Subject: an essay explaining how public-key cryptography works
raw:
If I want to explain public-key cryptography, the last thing I reach for is a padlock. The usual story has Alice mailing an open padlock to Bob, who snaps it shut on a box that only Alice can open. Fair enough, as an account of how to send somebody a locked box. But the most interesting thing my browser did this morning was nearly the opposite: it made a secret with a stranger without either party sending the secret at all. I think we teach the subject backwards by starting with encryption. Start with agreement.

Take the prime number 23. Start at 1, keep multiplying by 5, and after each multiplication keep only the remainder on division by 23. The first few stops are 5, 2, 10, 4, 20, 8. I can tell you where I stopped without telling you how many steps I took. In this example that distinction buys me approximately thirty seconds of privacy and rather less if you have a pencil. With a suitably chosen group of enormous size, though, counting the steps backwards from the answer is a genuinely nasty problem. Going forwards is cheap: to take sixteen steps I don’t need sixteen multiplications. I can square 5, square the result, square again, and square once more.

Now for the bit worth doing on paper. I secretly choose six steps and publish my result, 8. You secretly choose fifteen and publish yours, 19. I take your 19 and raise it to my private sixth power, again keeping only the remainder. You raise my 8 to your private fifteenth power. We both get 2. There is no coincidence here: I computed five to the power of fifteen times six; you computed five to the power of six times fifteen. A listener got both our postcards. Neither postcard said 2.

That is the trick Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman published in 1976, with numbers here diminished to the scale of a pub receipt. The public key is the stop you announce; the private key is the step count you keep. In a common modern version called X25519 the arithmetic takes place on an elliptic curve, not among the powers of 5, but the essential courtesy of the mathematics survives: my secret operation applied to your public result gives the same answer as your secret operation applied to mine. The public value fits in 32 bytes. Our software feeds the shared result into a key derivation function rather than using the raw answer as a password.

There is one appalling omission. You and I have not been introduced.

Suppose the stranger on the other end is meant to be my bank. I can do immaculate mathematics with someone claiming to be my bank. We will arrive at a splendidly secret number together, which is scant consolation if I then tell that person my current-account balance and where to send it. This is why a web server ordinarily has two quite different sorts of private key in play during a fresh TLS 1.3 connection. One is for the fleeting business of agreement. The other signs a record of the handshake so far, including the public values we exchanged. A signature is something the holder of a private signing key can produce and anyone with the matching public key can check. Nobody has to keep the checking instructions secret. Nor does checking a signature consist, in general, of “decrypting with the public key,” a piece of antique RSA classroom patter I would gladly retire.

Who says the checking key belongs to the bank? A certificate says so, and a certificate is itself signed. Follow the signatures up far enough and you reach a key my browser or operating system has been told to trust. I find this the most honest detail in the entire apparatus. At the bottom of a beautiful pile of mathematics sits an administrative decision. Somebody put that root on a list. Somebody can take it off.

Once the introductions are over, public-key cryptography largely leaves the room. My statement, with its undignified succession of bakery purchases, comes down the wire protected by fast symmetric cryptography: each end knows the same traffic key for that direction. The payoff for the apparently extravagant business of making a fresh agreement is what happens after the connection ends. If both ends discard the ephemeral secrets and traffic keys, a thief who obtains the bank’s signing key next Thursday cannot use it to read a recording of this morning’s statement. The signing key vouched for an exchange; it was never a spare copy of the answer. That distinction, quite invisible from the little padlock once displayed beside a web address, is the part I wish we had put on the icon.
